explanation: Paragraph 1.2 of the Code prohibits a solicitor from abusing their position by taking unfair advantage of clients 'or others', which includes an opposing party. Paragraph 1.4 prohibits misleading clients, the court 'or others'. The proposed letter would tell an unrepresented sole trader, who has said he struggles with formal English, that he does not need a lawyer. It would impose an oppressive 24-hour deadline and ask him to accept interest far higher than the contract allows. SRA guidance gives discouraging an opponent from taking legal advice, oppressive and artificial time limits, and exploiting an opponent's lack of legal knowledge as examples of taking unfair advantage. It says that the obligation is heightened where the opponent is vulnerable or unrepresented. The firm may pursue the debt firmly and correspond with Mr Hussain directly. It must state the claim accurately, allow him a reasonable time to respond and not discourage him from seeking advice.

why_wrong.A: The Code expressly protects 'others': para 1.2 forbids taking unfair advantage of them and para 1.4 forbids misleading them.
why_wrong.B: The label does not affect whether the content takes unfair advantage of, or misleads, the recipient.
why_wrong.C: A solicitor may act against an unrepresented party; what matters is that the solicitor does not take unfair advantage of them.
why_wrong.D: Nothing prevents a solicitor from corresponding directly with an unrepresented opponent, provided they do so fairly.

key_rule: A solicitor must not take unfair advantage of, or mislead, an opposing party; the duty is heightened where the opponent is unrepresented or vulnerable.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 1.2 and 1.4; SRA Principles 2 and 5

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: COLP's duty to report suspected alteration of a signed witness statement (Code for Firms 9.1)
scenario: Haverford Law LLP handles high volumes of personal injury claims. Its compliance officer for legal practice (COLP), Amina Yusuf, finds credible evidence during a file audit that an associate altered a client's witness statement after the client had signed it. The altered statement was then filed at court. The managing partner wants to wait for the outcome of an internal disciplinary hearing in three months' time before deciding whether to tell anyone outside the firm, to protect the firm's reputation.
stem: What does the SRA Code of Conduct for Firms require of Amina?

options.A: She must take all reasonable steps to ensure that a prompt report is made to the SRA of the facts, which she reasonably believes are capable of amounting to a serious breach.
options.B: She should wait for the internal disciplinary outcome, because a report is needed only once a serious breach has been proved.
options.C: She need take no action, because reporting breaches by individuals is the responsibility of the compliance officer for finance and administration (COFA).
options.D: She need only notify the court, because the misconduct concerns a document filed in proceedings.
options.E: She need only report if the client complains about the altered statement.

explanation: Paragraph 9.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Firms requires a COLP to take all reasonable steps to ensure that a prompt report is made to the SRA of any facts or matters that they reasonably believe are capable of amounting to a serious breach of the SRA's regulatory arrangements by the firm, its managers or its employees. The test is not that a breach has been proved. It is a reasonable belief that the facts are capable of amounting to a serious breach. Credible evidence that a signed witness statement was altered and filed at court suggests possible dishonesty and misleading the court. That is capable of being a serious breach (Code for Solicitors paras 1.4 and 2.2; Principles 1, 4 and 5). Waiting three months for an internal process would not be 'prompt'. Concern for the firm's reputation is no reason to delay. The firm itself has parallel duties under paras 3.9 and 3.11, and must not subject anyone to detrimental treatment for reporting (para 3.12).

why_wrong.B: The trigger is a reasonable belief that facts are capable of amounting to a serious breach, not proof; delaying for three months would not be prompt.
why_wrong.C: The COFA's reporting duty concerns the SRA Accounts Rules; reporting other serious breaches is the COLP's responsibility under para 9.1.
why_wrong.D: Whatever steps are needed in the proceedings, the Code for Firms separately requires a prompt report to the SRA.
why_wrong.E: The duty does not depend on any complaint by the client.

key_rule: A COLP must take all reasonable steps to ensure a prompt report to the SRA of facts reasonably believed capable of amounting to a serious breach; proof is not required first.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Firms, paras 3.9, 3.12 and 9.1(d)

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Client wants to leave a significant gift to the solicitor drafting the will (Code 6.1)
scenario: Edwin Thorne, aged 81, is a long-standing client of Clara Jennings, a solicitor. He asks her to prepare a new will leaving her his holiday cottage, worth about £250,000, to thank her for years of help. His estate is worth about £900,000. Clara is not related to him. She has no doubts about his capacity, but he says he does not want 'any more lawyers involved'.
stem: How should Clara proceed?

options.A: She may prepare the will, because Mr Thorne has capacity and his wishes are clear.
options.B: She may prepare the will, provided another solicitor in her firm supervises its signing.
options.C: She may prepare the will, provided it is witnessed by two independent people.
options.D: She should satisfy herself that Mr Thorne has first taken independent legal advice about the gift; if he will not, she will usually need to cease acting on the will.
options.E: She may prepare the will, provided she undertakes to disclaim the gift if his family objects after his death.

explanation: Paragraph 6.1 of the Code prohibits a solicitor from acting where there is an own interest conflict or a significant risk of one. There are no exceptions, so client consent cannot cure it. The SRA's guidance on drafting and preparing wills says that where a client wishes to make a gift of significant value to the solicitor (or a family member or colleague), the solicitor should satisfy themselves that the client has first taken independent legal advice about the gift. 'Significant value' covers a gift that is significant in itself or significant relative to the estate. A cottage worth £250,000 is significant on both measures. Clara's personal financial interest conflicts with her duty to advise Mr Thorne impartially. She should explain this and ask him to take independent advice from another firm. The guidance says that if the client does not agree to take independent advice, the solicitor will usually need to cease acting.

why_wrong.A: Capacity and clear wishes do not remove the own interest conflict created by a significant gift to the drafting solicitor.
why_wrong.B: Supervision of execution by a colleague in the same firm is not independent legal advice and does not remove the conflict.
why_wrong.C: Valid execution goes to the will's formal validity, not to whether Clara may act despite her own interest in the gift.
why_wrong.E: A promise to disclaim later does not remove the conflict at the time she drafts the will and advises him.

key_rule: Before drafting a will containing a significant gift to themselves, a solicitor should be satisfied the client has taken independent legal advice; if the client refuses, they will usually need to stop acting.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.1; SRA guidance, Drafting and preparation of wills (updated 25 November 2019)

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Solicitor drafting a parent's will that leaves residue equally to the solicitor and siblings
scenario: Jonah Feld, a solicitor, is asked by his widowed mother to prepare a new will. It will make the same main provision as her existing will, which another firm drafted: her residuary estate is to pass to her three children, including Jonah, in equal shares. There are no unusual gifts. His siblings know of their mother's wishes and agree with them. His mother has full capacity and does not want to pay another firm.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Jonah may draft the will without his mother first taking independent legal advice?

options.A: He must refuse, because a will that benefits the drafting solicitor always requires the client to take independent legal advice first.
options.B: He may do so if, in the specific circumstances, he is satisfied that his financial interest and personal relationship do not undermine his ability to advise, and be seen to advise, impartially.
options.C: He may do so, provided his two siblings act as the attesting witnesses.
options.D: He may do so, because work for close relatives falls outside the SRA Code of Conduct.
options.E: He may do so, but only if he removes his own share of residue from the will.

explanation: Paragraph 6.1 of the Code prohibits acting where there is an own interest conflict or a significant risk of one. The SRA's wills guidance says that a solicitor drafting a will containing a significant gift to themselves should normally ensure that the client has first taken independent legal advice. However, the guidance accepts that there may be exceptions where the solicitor can continue without independent advice. Its example is a solicitor drafting a surviving parent's will that leaves the residuary estate to the solicitor and their siblings in equal shares. That is Jonah's situation. The provision is the even-handed division his mother already chose with another firm, and there is nothing unusual about it. Whether it is appropriate still depends on the circumstances, and Jonah must consider whether his financial interest or relationship undermines his ability to advise, and be seen to advise, impartially. He should keep a record of that judgement. If anything in the instructions departed from equal treatment in his favour, the position would change.

why_wrong.A: SRA guidance recognises exceptions, giving this very example: a surviving parent leaving residue to the solicitor and siblings in equal shares.
why_wrong.C: Witnessing would not address the conflict, and a gift to an attesting witness is generally void under s.15 Wills Act 1837.
why_wrong.D: The Code applies to work for relatives; the guidance treats this as a possible exception on the facts, not an exemption from the Code.
why_wrong.E: The guidance does not require him to forgo his share; the question is whether he can advise impartially in the circumstances.

key_rule: A solicitor may sometimes draft a parent's will leaving residue equally to the solicitor and siblings without independent advice, but only if their interest does not undermine their ability to advise impartially.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.1; SRA guidance, Drafting and preparation of wills

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Deceased client's son asks for her will and instructions before probate (Code 6.3)
scenario: Agnes Doyle has died. Her solicitors hold her will and their file of her instructions. Her executors are her two nieces. Her son, Patrick, who is not an executor, telephones the firm before probate has been granted. He asks for a copy of the will and an explanation of what his mother told the solicitor about why she left him only a small legacy.
stem: What should the solicitor do?

options.A: Give Patrick a copy of the will, because as her son he is her next of kin.
options.B: Refuse to give anything until the grant of probate, then send Patrick a full copy of the solicitor's file.
options.C: Treat the will and the file as confidential and disclose them only with the executors' consent, or where disclosure is otherwise required or permitted by law.
options.D: Give Patrick a brief summary of his mother's reasons, but not a copy of the will.
options.E: Disclose what he asks for, because the duty of confidentiality ended when Mrs Doyle died.

explanation: Paragraph 6.3 of the Code requires a solicitor to keep the affairs of current and former clients confidential unless disclosure is required or permitted by law or the client consents. The SRA's confidentiality guidance confirms that the duty continues after the client dies, and the right to confidentiality then passes to the client's personal representatives. Mrs Doyle's executors, her nieces, now control whether her will and her instructions may be disclosed. Patrick is neither the client nor a personal representative. The solicitor must not give him a copy of the will or any account of his mother's reasons unless the executors consent or some legal requirement or permission applies, such as a court order. The solicitor can politely explain the position and suggest that Patrick contact the executors or take his own legal advice.

why_wrong.A: Being next of kin does not give Patrick any right to the deceased client's confidential information; the right passes to her personal representatives.
why_wrong.B: The grant does not end confidentiality in the solicitor's file of instructions; disclosure still needs the personal representatives' consent or a legal basis.
why_wrong.D: A summary of her instructions is itself disclosure of confidential information without consent.
why_wrong.E: The duty continues after death; the right to confidentiality passes to the personal representatives.

key_rule: A solicitor's duty of confidentiality continues after a client's death; the right to confidentiality passes to the personal representatives, whose consent is needed for disclosure unless the law requires or permits it.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.3; SRA guidance, Confidentiality of client information (updated 30 June 2022)

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Joint owners selling: one co-owner's instruction to pay all the proceeds to her (Code 3.1 and 6.2)
scenario: A firm acts for Dev Malhotra and Fiona Grey, the registered proprietors of a flat, on its sale. They hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common in equal shares under a declaration of trust. They have recently separated. The day before completion, Fiona emails the firm instructing it to pay the whole net proceeds of sale into her sole bank account, because Dev owes her money. Dev knows nothing about this instruction.
stem: Which of the following best describes how the firm should proceed?

options.A: It should follow Fiona's instruction, because either joint client can give instructions that bind both.
options.B: It should pay all the proceeds to Dev, to protect him because he is unaware of the instruction.
options.C: It must pay the proceeds into court as soon as completion takes place.
options.D: It should pay the proceeds in equal shares under the declaration of trust, without telling either client about the disagreement.
options.E: It must not act on Fiona's instruction alone; it may deal with the proceeds only on instructions given or authorised by both clients and, as their interests now conflict over the proceeds, it must consider whether it can continue to act for both.

explanation: Paragraph 3.1 of the Code requires a solicitor to act only on instructions from the client, or from someone properly authorised to give instructions on their behalf. The firm's clients are Dev and Fiona jointly, and the proceeds are held for both of them. Fiona alone cannot authorise a payment that would defeat Dev's beneficial share. The firm must not follow her instruction without Dev's authority. Her email shows that the clients' interests now conflict over how the proceeds are distributed. Under para 6.2 the firm must not act on that aspect for both while there is a conflict or a significant risk of one. The 'substantially common interest' that justified acting for both in the sale does not extend to a dispute between them about the money. Each client is entitled to information material to their matter (para 6.4), so the firm should tell both of them about the position. It should hold the money pending joint instructions and consider whether it can continue to act for either or both.

why_wrong.A: Para 3.1 requires instructions from the client; where the firm acts for both co-owners, one cannot instruct it to act against the other.
why_wrong.B: Dev has given no such instruction either, and the firm cannot simply prefer one joint client over the other.
why_wrong.C: Payment into court is not the immediate step; the firm must first seek joint instructions and assess the conflict.
why_wrong.D: Acting without instructions and keeping both clients in the dark fails the firm's duties to act on instructions and keep each client informed.

key_rule: Where a firm acts for joint clients, it must not act on one client's instructions against the other's interests; once they disagree on an aspect, the firm must not act for both on it.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 3.1, 6.2 and 6.4

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Selling a house on the instructions of the owner's attorney under a registered LPA (Code 3.1)
scenario: Iris Penhale, aged 89, has advanced dementia and lacks capacity to manage her property and affairs. Her daughter, Morwenna, is her attorney under a registered lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs that contains no restrictions. Morwenna instructs a firm to sell her mother's house to pay care home fees. The firm has seen the registered LPA, and nothing suggests that Morwenna is acting other than in her mother's interests.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether the firm may act on the sale?

options.A: It may act on Morwenna's instructions, because she is properly authorised to give instructions on her mother's behalf, while remaining subject to the overriding obligation to protect Mrs Penhale's best interests.
options.B: It cannot act, because Mrs Penhale lacks capacity and so no one can give instructions for her.
options.C: It cannot act until the Court of Protection has appointed a deputy.
options.D: It may act only if Mrs Penhale signs the contract and transfer herself.
options.E: It may act only if all of Mrs Penhale's children consent to the sale.

explanation: Paragraph 3.1 of the Code requires a solicitor to act only on instructions from the client 'or from someone properly authorised to provide instructions on their behalf'. Mrs Penhale lacks capacity, but Morwenna holds a registered lasting power of attorney for property and financial affairs with no restrictions. That gives her authority to deal with her mother's property, including selling the house to pay for care. The firm has checked the registered LPA and has no reason to suspect that the instructions do not reflect Mrs Penhale's interests. Mrs Penhale remains the client, so the firm acts for her through her attorney. Paragraph 3.1 also says that where a solicitor has legal authority to act although the client's own instructions cannot be obtained, the solicitor is subject to the overriding obligation to protect the client's best interests. If concerns arose, such as the proceeds being diverted to the attorney, the firm would have to act on them.

why_wrong.B: Para 3.1 expressly allows instructions from someone properly authorised to give them on the client's behalf, such as an attorney acting within an LPA.
why_wrong.C: A deputy is not needed where a valid registered LPA for property and financial affairs already gives the attorney authority.
why_wrong.D: A client who lacks capacity cannot validly sign; the attorney signs within the scope of the power.
why_wrong.E: The authority to instruct belongs to the attorney under the LPA, not to the family collectively.

key_rule: A solicitor may act on instructions from someone properly authorised to give them, such as an attorney under a registered LPA, but must still protect the incapacitated client's best interests.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 3.1

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Firm's own error in a trust matter: openness and own interest conflict (Code 6.1, 7.11)
scenario: A firm acts for the trustees of the Ashdown family trust. Two years ago the trustees instructed the firm to invest £400,000 of trust money in line with a written investment strategy. An associate forgot, and the money has sat in a non-interest-bearing account ever since, causing the trust a significant loss. The trustees have not noticed. The supervising partner suggests either saying nothing and quietly investing the money now, or telling the trustees and asking them to sign a consent letter so that the firm can keep acting on all trust matters, including any claim arising from the error.
stem: Which of the following best describes what the firm should do?

options.A: Invest the money now and say nothing, because the trustees have not complained.
options.B: Tell the trustees and continue to act on every aspect, including any claim against the firm, once they give informed written consent.
options.C: Tell the trustees only if they later ask about the trust's investment returns.
options.D: Be honest and open with the trustees, explaining fully and promptly what happened and its likely impact and putting matters right if possible; it must not act where its own interests conflict with theirs, and their consent cannot cure that.
options.E: Write to the beneficiaries instead of the trustees, because the beneficiaries have suffered the loss.

explanation: Paragraph 7.11 of the Code requires a solicitor to be honest and open with clients if things go wrong. If a client suffers loss or harm as a result, the solicitor must put matters right if possible and explain fully and promptly what has happened and its likely impact. The firm must therefore tell the trustees about the uninvested money. Paragraph 6.1 prohibits acting where there is an own interest conflict or a significant risk of one. The SRA's conflicts guidance gives the firm's own conduct, such as wrong advice or the wrong action being taken, as an example. It says there are no exceptions: neither the client's consent nor telling the client to take independent advice changes the position. The firm cannot advise the trustees on a claim against itself, and it should recommend that they take independent advice on that. Whether it can keep acting on other trust work depends on whether its own interests create a significant risk of conflict on that work. Saying nothing and quietly investing the money would also breach Principles 4 and 5 (honesty and integrity).

why_wrong.A: The duty to be open when things go wrong does not depend on a complaint; concealment would also breach Principles 4 and 5.
why_wrong.B: There are no exceptions to the own interest conflict rule, so client consent does not allow the firm to advise on a claim against itself.
why_wrong.C: The firm must volunteer the information promptly, not wait to be asked.
why_wrong.E: The clients are the trustees, and the duties of openness and confidentiality are owed to them.

key_rule: When a firm's error causes a client loss, it must be open and explain promptly; it cannot act where its own interests conflict with the client's, and consent does not cure an own interest conflict.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 6.1 and 7.11; SRA guidance, Conflicts of interest

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Commission received from an insurer on a restrictive covenant indemnity policy (Code 4.1)
scenario: A firm acts for Leanne Choi on the sale of part of her land. The land is subject to an old restrictive covenant, and the buyer requires Ms Choi to provide a restrictive covenant indemnity insurance policy at her expense. The firm arranges the policy through a broker, and the insurer pays the firm £150 commission. The firm's client care letter says nothing about commissions.
stem: What must the firm do with the £150 commission?

options.A: Keep it, because it was paid by the insurer and not by Ms Choi.
options.B: Account to Ms Choi for it, unless she has agreed otherwise.
options.C: Keep it, because it is below a de minimis threshold.
options.D: Pay it to the buyer, because the buyer required the policy.
options.E: Keep it, provided it is shown on the final bill.

explanation: Paragraph 4.1 of the Code requires a solicitor to properly account to clients for any financial benefit received as a result of their instructions, except where the client has agreed otherwise. Paragraph 5.1 of the Code of Conduct for Firms imposes the same duty on the firm. The £150 commission is a financial benefit that the firm received only because it arranged the indemnity policy on Ms Choi's instructions and at her expense. It does not matter that the insurer, not Ms Choi, paid it. The firm must pay it to Ms Choi, for example by crediting it against her bill, unless she has agreed that the firm may keep it. Her agreement would need to be informed, so she would have to be told about the commission. The client care letter is silent and there is no such agreement, so the firm must account to her.

why_wrong.A: Para 4.1 covers any financial benefit received as a result of the client's instructions, whoever pays it.
why_wrong.C: Para 4.1 contains no de minimis threshold; the firm must account for any financial benefit unless the client has agreed otherwise.
why_wrong.D: The commission arose from Ms Choi's instructions and the policy was at her expense; the buyer is not the firm's client.
why_wrong.E: Showing it on a bill after the event is not the client agreeing that the firm may keep it.

key_rule: A solicitor must account to the client for any financial benefit, such as a commission, received as a result of the client's instructions, unless the client has agreed otherwise.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 4.1; SRA Code of Conduct for Firms, para 5.1

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Acting for seller and buyer of a flat where terms are still to be negotiated (Code 6.2)
scenario: Joy Baptiste wants to sell a buy-to-let flat to her long-standing tenant, Kofi Mensah. Both are existing clients of the same firm and want it to act for both of them to save costs. They have agreed a price of £240,000. They have not yet agreed who will pay for replacing a defective roof, how the tenancy deposit will be dealt with or the completion date, and they expect to negotiate these points.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether the firm may act for both?

options.A: Yes, because a seller and buyer have a substantially common interest in getting the sale completed.
options.B: Yes, provided both give informed consent, given or evidenced in writing.
options.C: No: because substantive negotiations between them are foreseen there is a significant risk of conflict, and neither the 'substantially common interest' nor the 'competing for the same objective' exception applies to a seller and buyer negotiating against each other.
options.D: Yes, provided different fee earners act for the seller and the buyer.
options.E: Yes, because the conflict rules do not apply to conveyancing once the price has been agreed.

explanation: Paragraph 6.2 of the Code prohibits acting where there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, unless the clients have a substantially common interest or are competing for the same objective, and the conditions on consent, safeguards and reasonableness are met. The SRA's conflicts guidance lists one client selling an asset to another client as a situation that can create a conflict. It says this does not mean you can never act, if on the facts there is no significant risk of conflict, for example where all the relevant terms are already agreed. However, if substantive negotiations between the clients are foreseen, the solicitor should not act unless an exception applies, because a conflict is likely. Ms Baptiste and Mr Mensah still have to negotiate the roof, the deposit and the completion date. A seller and buyer bargaining against each other are not competing for the same objective, and lack the strong consensus that a substantially common interest requires. The firm must act for only one of them, or for neither.

why_wrong.A: A substantially common interest requires a clear common purpose and strong consensus on how to achieve it; outstanding negotiations show there is no such consensus.
why_wrong.B: Consent is only one condition of an exception; it cannot authorise acting where no exception applies.
why_wrong.D: Separate fee earners may protect confidential information but do not create an exception to para 6.2.
why_wrong.E: There is no such carve-out; the conflict rules apply to conveyancing as to any other matter.

key_rule: A firm should not act for both seller and buyer where substantive negotiations between them are foreseen; neither 6.2 exception fits parties bargaining against each other, and consent alone cannot cure this.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.2; SRA guidance, Conflicts of interest

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Acting for buyer and lender when the buyer hides a cash-back from the lender (Code 1.4, 6.2)
scenario: A firm acts for Ollie Brennan on his purchase of a house for £300,000 and also for his mortgage lender. The lender's instructions, which the firm has accepted, require it to report any price reduction, cash-back or other incentive. Shortly before exchange, Ollie tells the solicitor that the seller has privately agreed to pay him £15,000 in cash after completion. The lender has been told only that the price is £300,000. Ollie says the solicitor must not tell the lender.
stem: Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?

options.A: She may continue, because a payment made after completion is a private matter between buyer and seller.
options.B: She may continue to act for both and simply report the cash-back to the lender after completion.
options.C: She may continue for both, provided Ollie gives informed written consent to her keeping the information from the lender.
options.D: She should ask the seller's solicitor to inform the lender, so that she does not breach Ollie's confidentiality.
options.E: She must advise Ollie that the arrangement has to be disclosed to the lender; if he refuses, she must not continue in a way that misleads the lender and must stop acting for the lender, and in practice for Ollie too, while considering her money laundering and fraud reporting obligations.

explanation: When acting for both buyer and lender, the solicitor owes each client duties. Under para 6.4 the lender is entitled to all information material to its matter, and its instructions expressly require price incentives to be reported. Ollie's information is confidential to him (para 6.3) and he refuses consent to disclosure. Paragraph 1.4 prohibits misleading clients 'or others', including by omission or by being complicit in a client's acts. Carrying on and reporting a £300,000 price to the lender would mislead it. A conflict has now arisen between the two clients, and no exception in para 6.2 applies. The solicitor must advise Ollie that the arrangement must be disclosed. If he still refuses, she cannot continue to act for the lender and, in practice, will have to stop acting for him as well. An undisclosed incentive concealed from a lender is a classic mortgage fraud warning sign, so she must also consider her money laundering and reporting obligations.

why_wrong.A: The lender has expressly required incentives to be reported; staying silent would mislead it about the true price.
why_wrong.B: By then the lender will have advanced its money on a misleading basis; a report after completion does not prevent the lender being misled.
why_wrong.C: Consent from one client cannot authorise misleading the other; the conflict between buyer and lender has no applicable exception.
why_wrong.D: Using the other side to pass on the information does not resolve her own conflict or her duty not to mislead her lender client.

key_rule: A solicitor acting for buyer and lender must not mislead the lender about price incentives; if the buyer forbids disclosure, the solicitor must cease acting for the lender and, usually, the buyer.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 1.4, 6.2, 6.3 and 6.4

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Defending a client who has privately admitted guilt but wants to plead not guilty
scenario: Danny Fitch is charged with stealing £2,000 from his employer's till. In a private conference he tells his solicitor that he took the money, but says he wants to plead not guilty because he thinks the CCTV evidence is poor quality.
stem: Which of the following best describes how the solicitor may proceed?

options.A: She may continue to act on a not guilty plea and put the prosecution to proof of its case, but must not mislead the court, for example by advancing a positive defence she knows to be false or calling Danny to deny the theft on oath.
options.B: She must stop acting immediately, because she cannot represent a client who has admitted guilt.
options.C: She must inform the court of Danny's admission, because her duty to the court overrides her duty to her client.
options.D: She may run an alibi defence if Danny can find witnesses to support it.
options.E: She must enter a guilty plea on Danny's behalf, because she knows the truth.

explanation: It is a defendant's right to require the prosecution to prove its case, and the client cannot be prevented from pleading not guilty, even after admitting guilt to their solicitor. The SRA's paper on balancing duties in litigation confirms that the admission remains covered by confidentiality (Code para 6.3) and legal professional privilege. The solicitor may therefore continue to act. She can test the prosecution evidence, for example by challenging the identification from the CCTV, and argue that the evidence does not prove guilt to the criminal standard. She must not mislead the court (para 1.4) or put forward assertions that are not properly arguable (para 2.4). She cannot suggest that Danny did not take the money, run a positive defence she knows to be false, or call him to give evidence denying the theft. The SRA paper says that if a client continues to mislead the court despite advice, the solicitor should cease to act.

why_wrong.B: A client who has admitted guilt may still plead not guilty and require the prosecution to prove its case; the solicitor may act within limits.
why_wrong.C: The admission is confidential and privileged; the duty not to mislead does not require her to disclose it.
why_wrong.D: Advancing an alibi she knows to be false would mislead the court and could involve fabricating evidence.
why_wrong.E: The plea is the client's decision; a solicitor cannot enter a plea against the client's instructions.

key_rule: A solicitor may defend a client who has admitted guilt by putting the prosecution to proof, but must not mislead the court by advancing a positive case or evidence known to be false.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 1.4, 2.4 and 6.3; SRA, Balancing duties in litigation (2018)

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Sentencing where the prosecution wrongly states the client has no previous convictions
scenario: Kyle Moran pleads guilty in the magistrates' court to criminal damage. At sentencing, the prosecutor tells the bench that he has no previous convictions, because his record from another police area has not been found. Earlier, Kyle told his solicitor in confidence that he has two previous convictions for similar offences. He instructs her to tell the magistrates in mitigation that he is a man of good character.
stem: Which of the following best describes the solicitor's position?

options.A: She must tell the bench about the two convictions, even without Kyle's consent, because her duty to the court overrides confidentiality.
options.B: She may follow Kyle's instructions, because the prosecution, not the defence, is responsible for the accuracy of the record.
options.C: She may say that Kyle is of good character, provided she does not refer to the prosecution's statement.
options.D: She must not tell the court that Kyle is of good character or otherwise mislead it; she may not reveal his convictions without his consent; and if he insists that she present him as of good character, she must cease to act.
options.E: She must withdraw at once and tell the bench that she is doing so because her client has previous convictions.

explanation: Paragraph 1.4 of the Code prohibits a solicitor from misleading the court, whether by her own acts or by being complicit in her client's. Paragraph 6.3 requires her to keep her client's affairs confidential unless disclosure is required or permitted by law or the client consents. Telling the magistrates that Kyle is of good character, when she knows he has two similar convictions, would be a deliberate falsehood, so she must refuse. Her duty of confidentiality also means she must not reveal the convictions without his consent. She should advise Kyle of her position and explain the risk of the record later coming to light. She may still mitigate on matters that are true, such as the guilty plea, remorse or personal circumstances, without referring to his character. If Kyle insists that she present him as of good character, she cannot continue and must cease to act. She must not tell the court why she is withdrawing.

why_wrong.A: The information is confidential (para 6.3) and she may not disclose it without consent; her duty is not to mislead, not to inform against her client.
why_wrong.B: Positively asserting good character that she knows to be false would mislead the court, whoever made the original error.
why_wrong.C: Any assertion of good character she knows to be untrue misleads the court, however it is phrased.
why_wrong.E: If she withdraws she must not reveal the confidential reason; and she need not withdraw if she can mitigate without misleading the court.

key_rule: A defence solicitor must not assert a client's good character knowing it to be false, nor disclose the client's convictions without consent; if the client insists on the falsehood, the solicitor must cease to act.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 1.4 and 6.3; SRA Principle 1

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Co-defendants whose accounts conflict: acting for both (Code 6.2 and 6.5)
scenario: A firm represents Leon Carter and Mason Reid, who are jointly charged with robbery. At first both deny any involvement. In a later private consultation Leon tells the firm that Mason planned the robbery and carried the knife, and that he intends to say so in his defence statement and at trial. Mason maintains a complete denial and has given the firm confidential details of his own account.
stem: Which of the following best describes the firm's position?

options.A: It may continue to act for both, because co-defendants have a substantially common interest in being acquitted.
options.B: It must not continue to act for both; it may continue for one only if it holds no confidential information of the other material to the matter, or the paragraph 6.5 conditions are met; otherwise it must cease acting for both.
options.C: It may continue to act for both if both give informed consent, given or evidenced in writing.
options.D: It may continue to act for both, provided a different fee earner handles each client.
options.E: It must continue to act for Mason, because he instructed the firm first.

explanation: Paragraph 6.2 of the Code prohibits acting where there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, unless the clients have a substantially common interest or are competing for the same objective. Leon now intends to blame Mason, who denies everything. The firm would have to challenge Mason's account for Leon while defending Mason against Leon's allegations. That is a direct conflict, and neither exception applies. The firm cannot continue to act for both. Once it stops acting for one, that person becomes a former client whose confidential information the firm holds. Under para 6.5, the firm may then act for the other, whose interests are adverse, only if effective measures mean there is no real risk of the information being disclosed, or the former client gives informed written consent. Mason has given the firm confidential details of his account, and Leon's information is equally material, so the firm is likely to have to stop acting for both.

why_wrong.A: Their defences are now directly opposed: Leon's defence blames Mason, so there is no strong consensus on how to achieve their aims.
why_wrong.C: Consent is only a condition of a para 6.2 exception, and no exception applies to defendants running defences against each other.
why_wrong.D: Separate fee earners do not create an exception to the conflict; the firm would still be acting for clients with opposing interests.
why_wrong.E: The order of instructions is irrelevant; the question is whether the firm can act for either without misusing the other's confidential information.

key_rule: A firm cannot act for co-defendants whose defences conflict; it may keep one only if it holds no material confidential information of the other or the para 6.5 conditions are met.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 6.2, 6.3 and 6.5

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Privileged advice mistakenly sent by seller's solicitor: must the buyer be told? (Code 6.4(d))
scenario: Zainab Ali, a solicitor, acts for the buyer of a commercial unit. The seller's solicitors email her a set of replies to enquiries and mistakenly attach a letter of advice from the seller's counsel. The letter discusses a serious flooding risk that is not mentioned in the replies. Zainab realises at once that it is a privileged document that was sent to her by mistake.
stem: Under paragraph 6.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, is Zainab obliged to tell her client what the letter says?

options.A: Yes, because she must make her client aware of all information material to the matter of which she has knowledge.
options.B: Yes, but only if the client signs a written waiver of any claim against the seller first.
options.C: No: the duty to make the client aware of all material information does not apply where the information is contained in a privileged document that she knows of only because it was mistakenly disclosed.
options.D: Yes, but only after exchange of contracts, so that the transaction is not disrupted.
options.E: Yes, but she may tell the client orally and must not send the letter itself.

explanation: Paragraph 6.4 of the Code requires a solicitor acting for a client to make the client aware of all information material to the matter of which the solicitor has knowledge, subject to limited exceptions. Paragraph 6.4(d) excludes information 'contained in a privileged document that you have knowledge of only because it has been mistakenly disclosed'. Counsel's advice to the seller is privileged. Zainab knows its contents only because it was attached by mistake, and she realised this at once. So para 6.4 does not oblige her to tell her client what it says. The exception reflects the importance the law attaches to legal professional privilege. In practice she should tell the seller's solicitors about the error and not use the document. She remains free to protect her client by proper means, for example by raising general enquiries and arranging searches and surveys about flood risk, as she would in any commercial purchase.

why_wrong.A: Para 6.4(d) creates an express exception for information in a privileged document known only because it was mistakenly disclosed.
why_wrong.B: No such waiver features in para 6.4; the exception in 6.4(d) applies regardless.
why_wrong.D: The timing is irrelevant; para 6.4(d) means there is no duty to pass on the contents at all.
why_wrong.E: The method of passing on the information does not matter; the 6.4 duty does not arise for this information.

key_rule: The Code duty to tell the client all material information does not extend to information in a privileged document the solicitor knows of only because it was mistakenly disclosed.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.4(d)

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Paying an agency for referrals of defendants awaiting trial (Code 5.1(d))
scenario: A criminal defence firm is approached by an agency that offers to refer defendants who have been charged and are awaiting trial in the Crown Court. The firm would pay the agency £100 for each client referred. The agency says the clients would be told about the payment and that the arrangement would be recorded in a written agreement.
stem: May the firm enter into this arrangement?

options.A: Yes, provided each client is told about the payment.
options.B: Yes, provided the arrangement is set out in a written agreement.
options.C: Yes, provided the payments come from the firm's profit costs and not from legal aid funds.
options.D: No, because the firm must not make payments to an introducer in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings.
options.E: Yes, but only for clients who are paying privately.

explanation: Paragraph 5.1 of the Code regulates referrals and introductions. Generally, clients must be told about any financial interest an introducer has, and any fee sharing agreement must be in writing. Paragraph 5.1(d), however, is an outright prohibition: a solicitor must not receive payments relating to a referral, or make payments to an introducer, in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings. Defendants who have been charged and are awaiting trial in the Crown Court are clearly the subject of criminal proceedings. The proposed £100 per client would be a payment to an introducer for referring them. Transparency with clients, a written agreement and the source of funding do not matter, because the protections in paras 5.1(a) to (c) apply only to arrangements that are permitted in the first place. Paragraph 7.1(b) of the Code of Conduct for Firms applies the same rule to the firm itself.

why_wrong.A: Telling the client cannot make lawful a payment that para 5.1(d) prohibits outright in criminal cases.
why_wrong.B: A written agreement is required for permitted fee sharing, but it does not authorise a referral payment that is prohibited.
why_wrong.C: The prohibition in para 5.1(d) applies however the payment is funded.
why_wrong.E: Para 5.1(d) covers all clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings, whether privately funded or legally aided.

key_rule: A solicitor or firm must not make or receive referral payments in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings, whatever disclosure or written terms are offered.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 5.1(d); SRA Code of Conduct for Firms, para 7.1(b)

subject: Land Law
title: Oral short lease at a market rent creates a legal lease (LPA 1925 s.54(2))
scenario: Harriet owns the freehold of a lock-up shop in Leicester, England. In March 2026 she orally agreed to let the shop to Kwame for three years at the best rent reasonably obtainable, with no premium. Kwame moved in the next day and pays the agreed monthly rent. Nothing was put in writing.
stem: Which of the following best describes the interest Kwame holds?

options.A: An equitable lease only, because a legal estate can be created only by deed.
options.B: A tenancy at will only, because an interest in land created orally has the force of an interest at will.
options.C: A legal lease for three years, because a lease taking effect in possession for not more than three years at the best rent, without a premium, can be created orally.
options.D: No interest at all, because a contract for a disposition of an interest in land must be in writing signed by both parties.
options.E: A legal lease, but only once it is completed by registration at HM Land Registry.

explanation: Section 52(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925 requires a deed to create a legal estate, but s.52(2)(d) excepts leases not required by law to be made in writing. Section 54(2) provides that nothing in the preceding provisions affects "the creation by parol of leases taking effect in possession for a term not exceeding three years" at the best rent reasonably obtainable without taking a fine (a premium). Kwame's lease meets each condition: it is for exactly three years, it took effect in possession immediately, it is at the best rent, and no premium was paid. It is therefore a legal lease even though it was made orally. Because it is a grant of the lease itself, not a contract to grant one, the writing requirement for contracts does not arise, and s.2(5)(a) of the 1989 Act in any case excludes contracts to grant such short leases. A three-year lease is not a registrable disposition.

why_wrong.A: The deed requirement in s.52(1) does not apply to leases within s.54(2), which can be created orally at law.
why_wrong.B: Section 54(1) yields to the express exception in s.54(2) for short leases at the best rent in possession.
why_wrong.D: Section 2 of the 1989 Act governs contracts, not the grant itself, and s.2(5)(a) excludes contracts for s.54(2) leases anyway.
why_wrong.E: Only leases of more than seven years (and certain others) must be completed by registration; a three-year lease is not one of them.

key_rule: A lease taking effect in possession for not more than three years, at the best rent reasonably obtainable without a premium, can be created orally and takes effect as a legal lease.
authority: Law of Property Act 1925, ss.52(2)(d) and 54(2)

subject: Land Law
title: Contract for the sale of land must be signed by both parties (LP(MP)A 1989 s.2)
scenario: Owen agreed to sell a field in Shropshire, England, to Priya for £85,000. Owen's solicitor prepared a single document setting out every term the parties had agreed. Owen signed it and sent it to Priya, who read it, telephoned Owen to say she was happy with it, but never signed it or any other copy. No deposit has been paid and neither party has acted on the arrangement. Owen now has a better offer and wants to withdraw.
stem: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.A: There is no contract, because the document incorporating the terms was not signed by or on behalf of Priya.
options.B: There is a contract, but it is enforceable only against Owen, because he is the party who signed.
options.C: There is a contract, because all the agreed terms were incorporated in one written document.
options.D: There is a contract, because Priya's oral acceptance by telephone completed the agreement.
options.E: There is a contract, but it cannot be enforced until Priya pays a deposit.

explanation: Under s.2(1) of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land can only be made in writing, incorporating all the expressly agreed terms in one document (or in each part where contracts are exchanged). Section 2(3) adds that the document must be signed by or on behalf of each party to the contract. Owen's document contains all the terms, but only Owen signed it. Priya's telephone call cannot supply the missing signature. Because s.2 states the conditions under which a contract "can only be made", the result is not an unenforceable contract but no contract at all, so Owen is free to withdraw. Nothing in the facts suggests a resulting or constructive trust or estoppel, which s.2(5) preserves: no money was paid and neither party relied on the arrangement.

why_wrong.B: This reflects the old s.40 LPA 1925 approach; s.2 requires signature by each party for any contract to exist.
why_wrong.C: Incorporating all terms in one document satisfies s.2(1) only; s.2(3) also requires both parties' signatures.
why_wrong.D: An oral acceptance cannot create a contract for the sale of land; the writing and signature requirements are mandatory.
why_wrong.E: Payment of a deposit is not a statutory condition of a land contract and cannot cure a missing signature.

key_rule: A contract for the sale of an interest in land can only be made in writing, incorporating all expressly agreed terms, signed by or on behalf of each party.
authority: Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, s.2(1) and (3)

subject: Land Law
title: Chattel or part of the land: degree and object of annexation (Elitestone v Morris)
scenario: Gethin has exchanged contracts to sell his freehold smallholding in Herefordshire, England, to Laila. The contract says nothing about a timber cabin in the orchard. The cabin was built on site about 30 years ago from timber frame panels and feather boarding. It rests by its own weight on concrete blocks set in the ground and is not bolted down. It has been used as a holiday home, and it cannot be taken down and rebuilt elsewhere: it could be removed only by demolishing it. Before completion, Gethin tells Laila that the cabin is his personal property and that he intends to sell it separately.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether the cabin passes to Laila on completion?

options.A: It does not pass, because an object resting on the land by its own weight alone always remains a chattel.
options.B: It does not pass, because Gethin regarded the cabin as his personal property and his intention decides the question.
options.C: It passes only if the contract expressly lists it, because structures not mentioned in the contract remain the seller's.
options.D: It passes, because the degree and object of annexation show it became part of the land: it was built to stay on site and cannot be removed except by demolition.
options.E: It passes only if it is connected to mains water or electricity, because a physical connection is required.

explanation: Whether an object brought onto land has become part of it depends mainly on the degree of annexation and the object (purpose) of annexation, assessed objectively. In Elitestone Ltd v Morris [1997] UKHL 15 a bungalow resting by its own weight on concrete pillars was held to be part of the land. Lord Lloyd said that a house constructed so that it cannot be removed at all, save by destruction, cannot have been intended to remain a chattel. The House also held that the subjective intention of the parties is relevant only so far as it can be derived from the degree and object of annexation. Gethin's cabin was built on site as a dwelling, has stood for decades, and could be removed only by demolition. It is therefore part of the land and passes to Laila with the freehold, whatever Gethin now believes.

why_wrong.A: Absence of physical attachment is not decisive; in Elitestone a building resting by its own weight became part of the land.
why_wrong.B: Subjective intention is irrelevant except as shown by the degree and object of annexation.
why_wrong.C: Anything forming part of the land passes with it unless excluded; it need not be listed in the contract.
why_wrong.E: Service connections are not required; the bungalow in Elitestone was treated as not physically attached yet still formed part of the land.

key_rule: An object becomes part of the land according to the degree and object of annexation, judged objectively; a structure that can be removed only by demolition is part of the land.
authority: Elitestone Ltd v Morris [1997] UKHL 15; [1997] 1 WLR 687

subject: Land Law
title: First registration: gift of unregistered land not registered within two months (LRA 2002 ss.4, 6, 7)
scenario: In February 2026 Ifeoma, who owns an unregistered freehold house in Norwich, England, transferred it to her son Chidi as a gift by a deed of gift. Chidi did not apply to HM Land Registry for registration, and no application was made to extend the period for registration. In June 2026 Chidi asks his solicitor where the legal title now lies.
stem: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.A: Chidi holds the legal estate, but it is vulnerable to third parties until he registers it.
options.B: The transfer has become void as regards the legal estate, which has reverted to Ifeoma, who holds it on a bare trust for Chidi.
options.C: Registration was not required, because compulsory first registration is triggered only by a transfer for valuable consideration.
options.D: The gift has failed completely, so Ifeoma is again the absolute legal and beneficial owner.
options.E: Chidi still has time, because the period for registration is three months from the transfer.

explanation: Under s.4(1)(a)(i) of the Land Registration Act 2002, the requirement of registration applies on a transfer of a qualifying estate, including an unregistered freehold, "for valuable or other consideration, by way of gift" or under a court order. Section 6 requires the transferee to apply for registration within the period for registration, which s.6(4) sets at two months from the transfer unless the registrar extends it. Chidi made no application, so s.7(1) applies: the transfer becomes void as regards the transfer of a legal estate. Section 7(2)(a) provides that, in a case within s.4(1)(a), the title to the legal estate reverts to the transferor, who holds it on a bare trust for the transferee. Ifeoma therefore holds the legal estate on bare trust for Chidi, who keeps the whole beneficial interest. The legal title can be put right only by a fresh transfer followed by registration within time.

why_wrong.A: After the two-month period the transfer is void as regards the legal estate, so Chidi no longer holds it.
why_wrong.C: Section 4(1)(a)(i) expressly includes transfers by way of gift.
why_wrong.D: Section 7(2)(a) preserves Chidi's position: Ifeoma holds the legal estate on a bare trust for him, not as absolute owner.
why_wrong.E: The period for registration is two months, not three, under s.6(4).

key_rule: A transfer of unregistered freehold land, including a gift, must be registered within two months; otherwise the legal estate reverts to the transferor on a bare trust for the transferee.
authority: Land Registration Act 2002, ss.4(1)(a), 6(4) and 7(1)-(2)

subject: Land Law
title: Express easement over registered land operates at law only when registered (LRA 2002 s.27)
scenario: Sana is the registered proprietor of a freehold house in York, England. In January 2026 she granted her neighbour Tom, by deed, a right of way on foot and with vehicles over her driveway, for the benefit of Tom's registered freehold house, for ever. Tom paid £6,000 for the right. Neither party has made any application to HM Land Registry.
stem: Which of the following best describes the status of Tom's right of way at present?

options.A: It is a legal easement, because it was granted by deed for an interest equivalent to a fee simple.
options.B: It is a legal easement that overrides any later disposition of Sana's land, because legal easements are overriding interests.
options.C: It is void, because an easement over registered land cannot exist unless it is registered.
options.D: It is a mere licence, because it has not been entered on the register of Sana's title.
options.E: It takes effect in equity only, because the express grant of a legal easement over registered land does not operate at law until the registration requirements are met.

explanation: Section 27(2)(d) of the Land Registration Act 2002 makes the express grant of an interest falling within s.1(2)(a) of the Law of Property Act 1925 (an easement for an interest equivalent to a fee simple absolute in possession) a disposition that must be completed by registration. Under s.27(1), such a disposition "does not operate at law until the relevant registration requirements are met". Tom's right was granted expressly by deed and is perpetual, so it is capable of being legal, but until it is registered it takes effect only in equity. Until it is registered, as an unprotected equitable easement it is at risk of being postponed to a later registered disposition of Sana's land for value.

why_wrong.A: A deed is necessary but not sufficient over registered land; s.27(1) withholds legal effect until registration.
why_wrong.B: Only legal easements can override under Sch 3 para 3, and this one is not yet legal; an expressly granted easement should be registered.
why_wrong.C: The grant is not void; it operates in equity until registration.
why_wrong.D: A grant by deed for value of a right capable of being an easement creates a proprietary interest, at least in equity, not a mere licence.

key_rule: The express grant of a legal easement over registered land must be completed by registration; until then it does not operate at law and takes effect in equity only.
authority: Land Registration Act 2002, s.27(1) and (2)(d)

subject: Land Law
title: Protecting a beneficial interest under a trust of land: restriction, not notice (LRA 2002 s.33)
scenario: Ana and her brother Femi bought a freehold flat in Leeds, England, as an investment. Ana alone is the registered proprietor, but Femi paid half the price and they agreed in writing that he owns half the beneficial interest. Femi does not live at the flat, which is let to a tenant. Femi wants to make sure that Ana cannot sell or mortgage the flat without his interest being protected.
stem: Which entry should Femi seek on the register of Ana's title?

options.A: An agreed notice, because a notice is the usual way to protect a third-party interest in registered land.
options.B: A restriction, because no notice may be entered in respect of an interest under a trust of land.
options.C: A unilateral notice, because Ana is unlikely to consent to an agreed notice.
options.D: No entry, because his interest automatically overrides any disposition by Ana.
options.E: A caution against dealings, because his interest arises under a trust.

explanation: Section 33(a)(i) of the Land Registration Act 2002 provides that no notice may be entered in the register in respect of an interest under a trust of land. Femi's half share is a beneficial interest under a trust of land, so neither an agreed nor a unilateral notice is available. The correct protection is a restriction, which regulates the circumstances in which a disposition may be registered. Section 42(1)(b) recognises a restriction's purpose of securing that interests capable of being overreached on a disposition are overreached; in practice a restriction ensures that capital money is paid to at least two trustees, so that Femi's interest is overreached into the proceeds rather than lost. Femi cannot rely on an overriding interest, because he is not in actual occupation of the flat.

why_wrong.A: Section 33(a) prohibits any notice, agreed or unilateral, for an interest under a trust of land.
why_wrong.C: A unilateral notice is still a notice and is barred by s.33(a).
why_wrong.D: An interest can override under Sch 3 para 2 only if its owner is in actual occupation, and Femi is not.
why_wrong.E: New cautions against dealings cannot be entered under the 2002 Act; restrictions and notices replaced them.

key_rule: No notice may be entered for an interest under a trust of land; a beneficiary protects the interest by a restriction on the register.
authority: Land Registration Act 2002, ss.33(a) and 42(1)(b)

subject: Land Law
title: Actual occupation: occupier who fails to disclose her interest on inquiry (LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 2(b))
scenario: Dev is the sole registered proprietor of a freehold house in Bath, England. His partner, Rosa, contributed half the purchase price on the understanding that she would own half the house, and she has lived there with him ever since. Nothing about her interest appears on the register. Dev agreed to sell the house to Imran. Before exchange, Imran's solicitor wrote to Rosa at the house asking whether she claimed any interest in the property; Rosa, an adult who fully understood the question, replied in writing that she did not. The sale was completed, the purchase money was paid to Dev alone, and Imran was registered as proprietor. Rosa now claims a half share binding on Imran.
stem: Which of the following best describes Rosa's position against Imran?

options.A: Her interest binds Imran, because she was in actual occupation at the time of the disposition.
options.B: Her interest binds Imran, because the purchase money was paid to only one trustee, so her interest was not overreached.
options.C: Her interest binds Imran, because he had constructive notice of her occupation.
options.D: Her interest does not bind Imran, because inquiry was made of her before the disposition and she failed to disclose her right when she could reasonably have been expected to do so.
options.E: Her interest does not bind Imran, because an interest under a trust can be protected only by a restriction, and none was entered.

explanation: Imran's registered purchase for value postpones prior interests unless their priority is protected (s.29 LRA 2002), for example as an overriding interest within Schedule 3. Rosa's beneficial interest was not overreached, because the money was paid to Dev alone. Her occupation would ordinarily make her interest overriding under Sch 3 para 2. However, para 2(b) excepts "an interest of a person of whom inquiry was made before the disposition and who failed to disclose the right when he could reasonably have been expected to do so". Imran's solicitor asked Rosa directly before the disposition whether she claimed an interest, and she, an adult who understood the question, denied having one. She could reasonably have been expected to disclose it. Her interest therefore falls outside para 2, is not otherwise protected, and is postponed to Imran's registered title.

why_wrong.A: Actual occupation is not enough where the para 2(b) exception applies because she denied her interest when asked.
why_wrong.B: Non-overreaching explains why she needs another route, but it does not make her interest bind Imran once para 2 is excluded.
why_wrong.C: The doctrine of constructive notice does not govern priority in registered land; ss.29-30 and Sch 3 do.
why_wrong.E: A beneficiary's interest can override through actual occupation without any restriction; it fails here only because of para 2(b).

key_rule: An occupier's interest does not override a registered disposition if inquiry was made of the occupier beforehand and they failed to disclose the right when they could reasonably have been expected to.
authority: Land Registration Act 2002, s.29 and Sch 3 para 2(b)

subject: Land Law
title: Legal easement exercised within the year before a disposition overrides (LRA 2002 Sch 3 para 3)
scenario: In 1990, when both plots were unregistered, the owner of Plot A, in Chester, England, granted the owner of Plot B by deed a perpetual right to run foul drainage through an underground pipe across Plot A. Plot A was later registered, but the easement has never been entered on its register. Waste from the house on Plot B has flowed through the pipe every day. In May 2026 Nadia bought Plot A for value and was registered as proprietor. The pipe is entirely underground, there are no manholes or other visible signs of it on Plot A, and Nadia did not know about it. She now wants to remove the pipe.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Nadia is bound by the drainage easement?

options.A: She is bound, because the legal easement had been exercised in the year ending with the day of the disposition to her.
options.B: She is not bound, because the easement was not within her actual knowledge and would not have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection.
options.C: She is not bound, because the easement was not protected by a notice on the register of Plot A.
options.D: She is bound only if the owner of Plot B was in actual occupation of Plot A at the time of the disposition.
options.E: She is not bound, because an easement over registered land operates at law only once it is registered.

explanation: Under s.29 LRA 2002, Nadia's registered purchase for value takes subject to interests within Schedule 3. Para 3(1) makes a legal easement overriding, except one which at the time of the disposition was not within the purchaser's actual knowledge and would not have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection. Nadia did not know of the pipe and it could not be seen, so the exception in para 3(1) would apply on its own. But para 3(2) provides that the exception does not apply if the person entitled proves that the easement has been exercised in the period of one year ending with the day of the disposition. The pipe has carried waste from Plot B every day, so the easement was exercised throughout that year. It was granted by deed before Plot A was registered, so it is a legal easement and the registration requirement for new express grants over registered land did not apply to it. It therefore overrides and binds Nadia.

why_wrong.B: Lack of knowledge and invisibility bring the para 3(1) exception into play, but para 3(2) disapplies it because the easement was used within the year.
why_wrong.C: A legal easement within Sch 3 para 3 overrides without any entry on the register.
why_wrong.D: Actual occupation is the test under para 2, not para 3; legal easements override under their own paragraph.
why_wrong.E: Section 27 applies to express grants out of a registered estate; this easement was granted in 1990 over unregistered land and is already legal.

key_rule: A legal easement overrides a registered disposition unless unknown and not obvious on inspection, and that exception does not apply if the easement was exercised in the year before the disposition.
authority: Land Registration Act 2002, s.29 and Sch 3 para 3

subject: Land Law
title: Rectification against a registered proprietor in possession (LRA 2002 Sch 4)
scenario: When Caleb bought his registered freehold house in Exeter, England, in 2023, HM Land Registry mistakenly included in his title a three-metre strip of garden that belonged to his neighbour, Joan, and removed it from her title. Caleb did not know of the error, gave no misleading information, and took proper care throughout. Since moving in he has fenced the strip into his garden and used it every day. Joan has now discovered the mistake and applies to the registrar for the register to be altered to restore the strip to her title. Caleb does not consent.
stem: Which of the following best describes how the application will be dealt with?

options.A: The register must be altered, because the registrar must approve an application to correct a mistake unless there are exceptional circumstances.
options.B: The register cannot be altered, because the register is conclusive and Caleb is the registered proprietor.
options.C: The alteration cannot be made without Caleb's consent unless it would for some other reason be unjust not to make it, because Caleb is in possession and did not cause or contribute to the mistake by fraud or lack of proper care.
options.D: The register will be altered automatically, because Joan's title to the strip is older than Caleb's.
options.E: Only the court, and not the registrar, can alter the register to correct a mistake.

explanation: Altering the register to correct the mistake would prejudicially affect Caleb's title, so it is rectification within Sch 4 para 1 LRA 2002. Under para 5(a) the registrar may alter the register to correct a mistake, but para 6(2) provides that no alteration affecting the title of the proprietor of a registered estate in land may be made without the proprietor's consent "in relation to land in his possession" unless (a) he has by fraud or lack of proper care caused or substantially contributed to the mistake, or (b) it would for any other reason be unjust for the alteration not to be made. Caleb is in possession of the strip, has fenced it and uses it, and was not at fault. Unless Joan can show some other reason why it would be unjust not to alter the register, the strip stays with Caleb. The duty in para 6(3) to approve applications applies only where the registrar has power to make the alteration, and para 6(2) removes that power here.

why_wrong.A: The duty in para 6(3) arises only where the registrar has power to alter, and para 6(2) restricts that power against a proprietor in possession.
why_wrong.B: The register can be altered under Sch 4 to correct a mistake; it is not absolutely conclusive.
why_wrong.D: Age of title is irrelevant; Schedule 4 sets the conditions for rectification.
why_wrong.E: Para 5 gives the registrar power to alter the register to correct a mistake, as well as the court under para 2.

key_rule: Rectification against a registered proprietor in possession needs his consent unless he caused or substantially contributed to the mistake by fraud or lack of care, or it would be unjust not to rectify.
authority: Land Registration Act 2002, Sch 4 paras 1, 5 and 6

subject: Land Law
title: Unregistered land: unregistered estate contract void despite notice (LCA 1972 s.4(6))
scenario: In 2024 Martin, who owns an unregistered freehold field in Lincolnshire, England, granted his neighbour Grace an option to purchase the field, by a written agreement complying with all formalities. Grace did not register the option as a land charge. In August 2026 Martin sold and conveyed the legal estate in the field to Ellis for its full market price. Before completion Martin had told Ellis about Grace's option. Consider the position at completion of the conveyance to Ellis.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Grace can enforce her option against Ellis?

options.A: Yes, because Ellis had actual notice of the option before he bought.
options.B: Yes, because an option is an equitable interest that binds everyone except a bona fide purchaser of a legal estate for value without notice.
options.C: Yes, because Grace's option is an overriding interest.
options.D: No, but only because Ellis paid the full market price for the field.
options.E: No, because an unregistered estate contract is void against a purchaser for money or money's worth of a legal estate in the land.

explanation: Title to the field is unregistered, so the Land Charges Act 1972 governs. An option to purchase is an estate contract, registrable as a Class C(iv) land charge. Section 4(6) provides that an estate contract created after 1925 is void as against a purchaser for money or money's worth of a legal estate in the land charged with it, unless it is registered before completion of the purchase. Grace did not register, and Ellis bought the legal estate for money, so the option is void against him. His knowledge of the option is irrelevant: s.199(1)(i) of the Law of Property Act 1925 provides that a purchaser is not prejudicially affected by notice of a registrable matter that is void against him for non-registration. Grace's remedy is a personal claim against Martin for breach of the option contract.

why_wrong.A: Notice of an unregistered registrable land charge does not bind a purchaser: s.4(6) LCA 1972 and s.199(1)(i) LPA 1925.
why_wrong.B: The traditional doctrine of notice does not apply to registrable land charges such as estate contracts; registration governs.
why_wrong.C: Overriding interests are a registered-land concept; in unregistered land, estate contracts depend on land charge registration.
why_wrong.D: Section 4(6) requires only a purchaser for money or money's worth, not payment of full value.

key_rule: An estate contract (such as an option) not registered as a Class C(iv) land charge is void against a purchaser of a legal estate for money or money's worth, whatever notice the purchaser had.
authority: Land Charges Act 1972, s.4(6); Law of Property Act 1925, s.199(1)(i)

subject: Land Law
title: Severance by written notice, then survivorship (LPA 1925 ss.36(2), 196(3))
scenario: Asha, Ben and Carys bought a freehold house in Bristol, England, together as an investment. They are the registered proprietors and the transfer declares that they hold the house on trust for themselves as beneficial joint tenants. Ben and Carys live in the house; Asha lives elsewhere. On 1 September 2026 Asha signed a written notice addressed to Ben and Carys stating that she wished to sever the beneficial joint tenancy, and she pushed it through the letterbox of the house. Carys read it that evening. Ben died suddenly on 3 September 2026 without having read it. Ben left a will giving everything to his sister.
stem: Which of the following best describes who now holds the legal title and the beneficial interests in the house?

options.A: Legal title: Asha and Carys. Beneficial interests: Asha, Carys and Ben's sister, one third each as tenants in common.
options.B: Legal title: Asha and Carys as joint tenants. Beneficial interests: Asha one third and Carys two thirds, as tenants in common.
options.C: Legal title: Asha and Carys as joint tenants. Beneficial interests: Asha and Carys as beneficial joint tenants, because the notice was not effective against Ben, who never read it.
options.D: Legal title: Asha, Carys and Ben's personal representatives. Beneficial interests: one third each.
options.E: Legal title: Asha and Carys as joint tenants. Beneficial interests: Asha and Carys, one half each as tenants in common.

explanation: The legal estate is always held by co-owners as joint tenants on trust, and s.36(2) LPA 1925 forbids severance of a joint tenancy of the legal estate. On Ben's death his share of the legal title passed by survivorship, so Asha and Carys hold the legal title as joint tenants. In equity, s.36(2) allows a joint tenant to sever by giving the other joint tenants notice in writing of that desire. Under s.196(3), a notice is sufficiently served if left at the last-known place of abode of the person to be served, so Asha's notice was served on Ben and Carys when it went through the letterbox, whether or not Ben read it. Asha thereby became a tenant in common of one third. Ben and Carys remained beneficial joint tenants of the other two thirds between themselves, so on Ben's death his interest passed to Carys by survivorship and nothing passed under his will. Carys holds two thirds and Asha one third, as tenants in common.

why_wrong.A: Severance by Asha affected only her own share; Ben and Carys remained joint tenants between themselves, so survivorship operated and Ben's will had nothing to pass.
why_wrong.C: Under s.196(3) a notice left at the last-known place of abode is validly served; it need not be read.
why_wrong.D: The legal title cannot be severed and passes by survivorship; it does not vest in a deceased joint tenant's personal representatives.
why_wrong.E: Asha severed only her one-third share; the remaining two-thirds survived to Carys, so the shares are unequal.

key_rule: A beneficial joint tenancy can be severed by written notice, validly served if left at the recipient's last-known abode; severance affects only the severing party's share, and the legal title remains joint.
authority: Law of Property Act 1925, ss.36(2) and 196(3)

subject: Land Law
